Each future change to the sidecar contract (ADR-029/043) has to be made in three hooks, and they will keep disagreeing about what counts as review evidence.

`git symbolic-ref` is run without `stdio: "pipe"`, so on detached HEAD git's `fatal: ref HEAD is not a symbolic ref` goes to the hook's stderr. `symbolic-ref --short` also never returns "HEAD", so the `branch === "HEAD"` check at line 93 is dead code. During a rebase or on a detached worktree, every shutdown SendMessage prints a git fatal error into the hook output, even though the hook then allows the call. review-gate pipes stderr for the same call. The dead `"HEAD"` comparison suggests the author expected `rev-parse --abbrev-ref` behavior, which is what the sibling hooks use.

CLAUDE.md (repo root) says "`docs/adr/` — Architecture Decision Records. Every non-trivial decision gets an ADR." This adds a new blocking enforcement point (PreToolUse on SendMessage), a new escape hatch (`--force-shutdown`) and a new evidence rule with no ADR, while merge-gate's evidence model got ADR-029/043. The evidence contract (what counts as review proof for shutdown, how it relates to ADR-029 sidecar naming) isn't written down anywhere. That is how the filename-vs-hash mismatch went unnoticed, and ADR-043 calls this kind of doc-code drift a [DEFECT].

In an unquoted heredoc, `\"` is kept as-is, so the remote probe becomes `binary_path="$(command -v \"jq\" || true)"`. Inside `$(...)` that `\"` is a literal quote character, so `command -v` searches for a file named `"jq"` (quotes included). For every non-wrapper entry (jq, rg, ffmpeg, uv, gh…), `command -v '"jq"'` finds nothing, `binary_path` comes back empty, and the probe prints `missing_binary:jq` and exits 1. The first manifest entry (jq) then triggers `fail "Failed to validate runtime binary jq…"`, so verify fails on every deploy, even healthy ones. Commit 19091e242 introduced this; plain `"${binary}"` (no backslashes) was what it meant to write.

`gce_ssh` (gcloud compute ssh → OpenSSH with no `-n`) runs inside `while IFS= read -r entry_json; do … done <<< "${entries_json}"`. It inherits the loop's stdin and forwards all of it to the remote, so the remaining manifest entries are consumed after the first SSH call. Once the quoting bug is fixed, the first entry (jq) runs `gce_ssh`, ssh reads every remaining line of the here-string, and the next `read` hits EOF. The loop exits cleanly with only jq checked. gemini, gh, uv and the rest are never verified, and verify passes even if they are missing. The wrapper-path calls at lines 267/271 have the same problem. Fix: add `</dev/null` to gce_ssh, pass `--ssh-flag=-n`, or read entries on fd 3 or via mapfile.

The list of binaries to verify now comes from the CI runner's checkout (`${repo_root}/scripts/docker/runtime-binaries.json`), not from the manifest baked into the image. The in-image manifest is only checked with `test -f` and its contents are never read. verify.yml runs `actions/checkout@v4` with no ref, so it uses whatever branch the workflow was dispatched from, which can differ from the image built from `deployed_ref`. Verifying production (a daisy/main image) from daisy/dev, with a binary added or removed on dev, gives a false failure for the new binary or silently skips one the image actually ships. The old probe always checked the image against its own manifest.

`runtime_wrapper_bin="${OPENCLAW_RUNTIME_WRAPPER_BIN:-/opt/daisy/bin}"` is now read on the CI runner. The old probe read it inside the container, where the Dockerfile sets `ENV OPENCLAW_RUNTIME_WRAPPER_BIN`. If an image sets OPENCLAW_RUNTIME_WRAPPER_BIN to another directory (or the sandbox and app images differ), verify checks `/opt/daisy/bin/gemini` and reports a false missing-wrapper failure. It could also pass on a stale file at the default path. The image's own setting is ignored.

The sandbox-image probe used to run `sh -lc`, which matches how sandboxed agents run commands (`/bin/sh -lc` in src/agents/bash-tools.shared.ts:85; /etc/profile resets PATH). The new code uses `sh -c` and direct exec, so it no longer tests the PATH agents actually get. For the non-root `sandbox` user, Debian /etc/profile resets PATH to `/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin:…`, which drops `/opt/daisy/bin` from the Docker ENV PATH. A binary reachable only through the image ENV PATH now passes verify but is `command not found` when an agent calls it in the sandbox.

To make wrapper-backed binaries exec directly, the whole in-container probe was replaced with a host-side loop: one SSH and docker call per binary, a repo-side manifest, and runner-side env. The underlying fix was a one-line change in the old in-container script: run `"${binary_path}" args` instead of `sh -c "${resolved_smoke_command}"`. The broader rewrite is where the regressions above come from: the stdin-consuming ssh loop, the manifest source-of-truth change, the runner-side wrapper env, and the login-shell drop. It also adds about 170 lines of command builders. A narrow fix inside the single remote probe would avoid all of them and keep one round trip per target.

Each manifest entry now costs one IAP SSH session (two for wrapper entries), plus two more per target for the manifest and arch checks. In image mode each of those is also a `docker run --rm` container start. The old probe did all of this in a single SSH call. With 12 amd64 entries, that is about 15 IAP SSH sessions for the gateway and about 15 more, each with a cold container start, for the sandbox image. At several seconds per IAP handshake, verify gets minutes slower and is more exposed to transient IAP failures. Batching all non-wrapper checks into one remote script keeps it to one call per target.

`[[ "${smoke_suffix}" == *'\\'* ]]` treats the single-quoted `\\` as a literal two-character string, so it only rejects suffixes with two backslashes in a row. A single backslash gets through. The same pattern is copied at line 196. A manifest smoke like `gemini --flag a\b` passes the 'complex suffix' guard that was meant to reject it. `printf %q` then escapes it, so the command runs with arguments that differ from what the manifest author wrote, and the guard does not do what its condition claims.

`gce_ssh "${manifest_check_command}"` and `gce_ssh "${wrapper_test_command}"` run inside a function whose stdout is captured as `runtime_bins` / `sandbox_runtime_bins`. Their stdout is not redirected, so any gcloud/ssh banner text lands in the captured result. gcloud first-connection output, IAP warnings, or remote MOTD text written to stdout is mixed into the `arch=…`/binary listing that gets printed to the CI log. That is the contamination gce_ssh_lastline exists to prevent; its comment warns this can leak key material into CI logs.

`smoke_suffix="${smoke_command#${binary}}"` leaves `${binary}` unquoted inside the parameter-expansion pattern, so glob characters in the binary name are treated as patterns, not literal text. The same code is at line 188. A manifest binary name containing `*`, `?` or `[` strips a different prefix than the `case` match checked, so the wrong arguments get passed to the direct-exec smoke. Use `${smoke_command#"${binary}"}`.

The `image` branch of build_target_direct_exec_command copies, line for line, the prefix-strip, the forbidden-character check and the `read -a` + `%q` loop from build_direct_exec_smoke_command. The container branch never uses the `smoke_suffix`, `arg` and `smoke_args` locals it declares. Fixes to the suffix rules (for example the backslash pattern bug) have to be made twice and will drift. One helper that returns the escaped argument string, with each mode adding its own `docker exec T path` or `docker run --entrypoint path T` prefix, removes about 25 duplicated lines.

build_target_manifest_check_command, _arch_command, _wrapper_test_command, _shell_command and _direct_exec_command each repeat the same container/image `case`, differing only in the program and its arguments. Their `|| fail "Failed to build … command"` paths can't trigger, because mode is hard-coded at both call sites. About 100 lines of near-identical builders and dead error branches. A single `target_exec mode target program args…` helper (container: `sudo docker exec T program args`; image: `sudo docker run --rm --entrypoint program T args`) does the same job.

Each loop iteration starts three separate `printf | jq -r` pipelines to pull `.binary`, `.smoke` and `.install.wrapper.type` from the same entry. That is about 36 extra process forks per target for no benefit. One `jq -r '[.binary,.smoke,(.install.wrapper.type//"")]|@tsv'` before the loop, read with `IFS=$'\t' read -r binary smoke_command wrapper_type`, does the same job.

normalize_runtime_arch re-implements `normalize_arch` from scripts/docker/install-runtime-binaries.sh:11 (same amd64/x86_64 and arm64/aarch64 mapping). If the installer gains an architecture alias and verify doesn't, verify rejects a target that the installer supports. Moving the mapping into a small shared sourced file keeps the two in step.

CLAUDE.md points to AGENTS.md, which says: "Enforce Zero Trust, Least Privilege, and Test Driven (TDD) with Anti-Mock policies in planning and code development." The diff adds about 240 lines of new verification logic (command builders, suffix parsing, the per-entry loop) with no tests. Both high-severity bugs above (literal-quote `command -v` and the stdin-consuming ssh loop) would have been caught by a basic test that runs the generated probe or the loop against a fake multi-entry manifest. Without one, they only show up during a real staging or production verify.

Every InvalidOperationException is mapped to 404 "Mailbox not found", and all other SMTP/IMAP/crypto failures go unhandled and return 500. The new `SendMailFailed` resource key is never used. Several MailKit exceptions inherit from InvalidOperationException: ServiceNotAuthenticatedException, ServiceNotConnectedException, and SmtpClient's "no recipients" error. Any of these makes the API tell the user their mailbox doesn't exist. A bad SMTP password (AuthenticationException), an unreachable host (SocketException), a TLS mismatch (SslHandshakeException), a 5xx reply (SmtpCommandException) or a rotated data-protection key (CryptographicException) all escape as an unhandled 500 with no localized message.

The `_isSending` guard is set only after `await GetBodyAndContentTypeAsync()`, which makes JS interop calls. A second click during that await gets past the `if (_isSending) return;` check. The user double-clicks Send. The first click awaits `quillInterop.isEmpty` / `getHtml`, which yields to the event loop. The second click runs SendAsync while `_isSending` is still false, and the button isn't disabled because no render has happened yet. Both calls POST /api/mail/send and recipients get two copies.

The CC/BCC section can now be hidden again (d15c6ca removed the one-way reveal). `_cc` and `_bcc` keep their values while hidden, are still validated and sent, and their errors render only inside the hidden section. The user types an address in BCC, then collapses CC/BCC. The message is sent to that BCC recipient with nothing on screen showing it. If the hidden CC holds a typo, `_errors["cc"]` is set and SendAsync returns early, but the error div is inside the collapsed block. Send then appears to do nothing.

`ImapClient.GetFolder(SpecialFolder.Sent)` throws NotSupportedException when the server has neither SPECIAL-USE nor XLIST. The name-based `?? ... "Sent"` fallback never runs, and the outer catch drops the Sent copy silently. On an IMAP server without SPECIAL-USE (e.g. the GreenMail dev server, or older Dovecot/Courier setups), GetFolder throws instead of returning null. The fallback that was written for exactly these servers is skipped. Only a warning is logged and sent mail never shows up in Sent. Matching only the name "Sent" also misses "Sent Items" and "Sent Messages".

`getHtml` returns `quill.root.innerHTML`. In Quill 2 that is editor markup: bullet lists are `<ol><li data-list="bullet">` with `<span class="ql-ui">`, and formatting is carried in ql-* classes. It is not semantic HTML. The user writes a bullet list in rich-text mode and sends. The server sanitizer strips `data-list`, and there is no Quill CSS in the recipient's client, so the list arrives numbered. Indents and alignment are lost. Turndown also turns those lists into `1.` items when switching to Markdown. `quill.getSemanticHTML()` returns proper `<ul>`/`<ol>` and should be used instead.

`setHtml` assigns marked's output directly to `quill.root.innerHTML`. This bypasses Quill's clipboard conversion, so the editor model is out of sync with the DOM, and raw unsanitized HTML from Markdown is injected into the page. Switching Markdown→Rich with `- a\n- b` or a fenced code block produces `
    `/`
    ` that Quill 2 has no blots for. Formatting gets mangled, and undo history and `getText()`/`isEmpty()` can disagree with what is displayed. Typing `` in Markdown and switching modes runs the script (self-XSS). Use `quill.clipboard.dangerouslyPasteHTML(html)` or `setContents(quill.clipboard.convert({ html }))`.

The DataAnnotations on SendMailRequest (`[Required]`, `[MaxLength]`, `[RegularExpression("^(html|plain)$")]`) are never enforced: Program.cs has no `AddValidation()`, and the endpoint checks only `To`. `{"to":null}` throws NullReferenceException at `request.To.Length`, and `{"to":[null]}` throws at `email.Trim()`. A null Subject or plain Body makes MimeKit throw ArgumentNullException. All of these return 500. `contentType: "HTML"` passes and raw HTML is sent as text/plain. Body size is limited only by Kestrel's 30 MB default, not the declared 1 MiB.

If `SmtpRequiresAuth` is true but no SMTP password is stored, authentication is skipped without any log or error, and the send continues unauthenticated. A mailbox is created with RequiresAuth=true and an empty SMTP password. The server answers MAIL FROM with 530 "Authentication required", which escapes as an unhandled 500 with no hint about the cause. On a permissive relay the mail goes out unauthenticated, against the mailbox's own setting.

Every sent message is unconditionally appended to the IMAP Sent folder. Providers such as Gmail and Office 365 already save SMTP-submitted mail to Sent themselves. A Gmail or Outlook.com user sends a message. The provider files it in Sent and the service appends a second copy, so the Sent folder (and the future Sent page sync) shows every message twice.

HTML mail is sent as a single text/html part with no text/plain alternative. Text-only clients and screen readers that prefer text/plain get no readable body. HTML-only messages also score higher with SpamAssassin and similar filters (MIME_HTML_ONLY), so compose output is more likely to land in spam. MimeKit's `BodyBuilder { HtmlBody = ..., TextBody = ... }` builds multipart/alternative.

When DisplayName is null, the From display name falls back to `mailbox.Name`, which is the user's internal label for the mailbox. A mailbox labelled "Work Gmail" with no DisplayName sends as `"Work Gmail" <me@gmail.com>`. Recipients see the internal label as the sender's name. Leave the name empty (bare address) instead.

The error response body is read into `error` and never used. The server's specific 400/404 message (which address is invalid, mailbox not found) is replaced by a generic "Failed to send" toast. The server rejects an address the client accepted, or the mailbox was deleted in another tab. The user sees only "Failed to send email. Please try again." and retrying gives the same result. The dead `ReadAsStringAsync` call adds a pointless round-trip on the response stream.

`IsValidEmail` is copied verbatim in ComposeEndpoints.cs and Compose.razor. MailSendingService also redeclares the "MailboxSmtpPassword"/"MailboxImapPassword" purpose strings (now in 4 files) and re-implements EmailService's SMTP connect/auth/send flow. Client and server validators can drift, e.g. one adds `;` splitting or IDN handling, and then the UI accepts what the API rejects. A typo in any copy of a purpose string makes Unprotect throw CryptographicException. Move IsValidEmail into Feirb.Shared and add the mailbox purposes to the existing `DataProtectionPurposes` class.

In SwitchToRichTextAsync, `StateHasChanged()` + `await Task.Delay(50)` + the `if (!_quillInitialized)` init branch are dead or fragile. Quill is always initialized in OnAfterRenderAsync before the user can switch modes, and its container is only hidden with display:none, never removed. The 50 ms sleep is a timing guess that adds latency to every mode switch and opens another re-entrancy window: a fast second click on Markdown runs during the delay and reads stale Quill content. `setHtml` works on the hidden container, so it can be called directly with no render or delay.

Quill, marked and Turndown are loaded as synchronous, render-blocking `<script>` tags on every page of the app, even though only /compose uses them. Every app load, including login and inbox, has to download and parse the full Quill UMD bundle plus marked and Turndown from jsDelivr before blazor.webassembly.js starts, which slows startup. If the CDN is slow or blocked, the whole app stalls. Load them lazily from Compose (JS module import, or inject on first render), and add SRI hashes.

postCreateCommand installs `.[dev]`, but pyproject.toml (hatchling backend) defines no `[project.optional-dependencies] dev`; the `dev` extra only exists in setup.py, which hatchling ignores. So pytest, pytest-asyncio, mypy, black, ruff and types-requests are never installed. The container builds and uv only prints `warning: ... does not have an extra named dev`. Running `pytest` in the container then fails with command not found (or `No module named pytest`), and tests/test_server.py needs pytest-asyncio for its `@pytest.mark.asyncio` tests. README line 65 says it 'installs all Python dependencies automatically', which is false. The real fix is to add a `dev` extra to pyproject.toml that mirrors requirements-dev.in.

`workspaceFolder` and `python.defaultInterpreterPath` (line 20) hardcode `/workspaces/ProxmoxMCP-Plus` with no matching `workspaceMount`. The default mount target is `/workspaces/${localWorkspaceFolderBasename}`, so these paths only exist when the local folder is named exactly `ProxmoxMCP-Plus`. A user clones into a different folder (`git clone ... pmcp`, a renamed fork, or a checkout like this one named `repo`) and picks Reopen in Container. The repo gets mounted at `/workspaces/pmcp`, VS Code opens a folder that doesn't exist, and postCreateCommand fails because its working directory is missing. Use `${containerWorkspaceFolder}` / `/workspaces/${localWorkspaceFolderBasename}`, or drop workspaceFolder.

`uv venv` builds `.venv` inside the bind-mounted workspace. That is the same `.venv` the README's local install creates on the host, so the container replaces it with a Linux venv whose interpreter is a symlink to `/usr/local/bin/python3.11`. On every Rebuild Container it runs again against the venv the previous container left behind. A macOS/Windows developer followed the README's 'uv venv' steps on the host, then opens the Dev Container. Their host `.venv` is wiped and replaced. Back on the host, `.venv/bin/python` points at a path that doesn't exist and the host IDE and CLI break. Newer uv versions also move toward requiring `--clear` before replacing an existing env, so with unpinned uv a rebuild can start failing postCreate. Put the venv outside the workspace (e.g. `UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=/home/vscode/.venv`) or on a named volume.

postCreateCommand runs after VS Code has already attached (default `waitFor` is `updateContentCommand`), and nothing puts `.venv/bin` on PATH. The Python extension can resolve `defaultInterpreterPath` before `.venv` exists and fall back to `/usr/local/bin/python`, which leaves terminals without the venv. In a terminal opened after container start, `mcpo`, `pytest` and `python -m proxmox_mcp.openapi_proxy` use system Python, which doesn't have the package. `./start_openapi.sh` sees no `mcpo` on PATH, pip-installs it into ~/.local, then fails with `ModuleNotFoundError: proxmox_mcp`. Fix by setting `"waitFor": "postCreateCommand"` (or using onCreateCommand) and adding `remoteEnv.PATH` with the venv bin dir.

`apt-get install --no-install-recommends git` skips git's Recommends (`openssh-client`, `less`, `patch`). The container has git but no `ssh` binary, so SSH remotes don't work even though VS Code forwards the SSH agent. A contributor with a `git@github.com:` remote runs `git push` or `git fetch` in the container and gets `error: cannot run ssh: No such file or directory`. GitLens/Git Graph operations on that remote fail the same way. Add `openssh-client` (and `less`) explicitly.

`useradd` is called without `-s /bin/bash`. On Debian (python:3.11-slim) the user's login shell defaults to `/bin/sh` (dash), and VS Code opens integrated terminals with that shell. The developer opens a terminal and gets a bare dash prompt with no completion or history. The README's `source .venv/bin/activate` fails with `sh: 1: source: not found`. Use `useradd -s /bin/bash ...`.

Step 4 says the OpenAPI proxy 'is reachable at http://localhost:8811', but the Dev Container never starts it and the README never says to run `./start_openapi.sh` with the venv active. The container also doesn't set `PROXMOX_MCP_CONFIG`, so the config.json from step 3 is ignored unless the user runs that script. The user finishes steps 1-3 and opens localhost:8811: connection refused. Running `python -m proxmox_mcp.server` by hand ignores proxmox-config/config.json, falls back to PROXMOX_HOST and the other env vars, and fails config validation. In Codespaces the forwarded URL isn't localhost at all. Add a 'run ./start_openapi.sh' step and `containerEnv.PROXMOX_MCP_CONFIG`.

`editor.formatOnSave: true` with Black as the Python formatter is turned on for a codebase that isn't Black-formatted: 205 lines over 88 chars and 245 trailing-whitespace lines across 21 files in src/. There's also no Black config, and the extension's bundled Black version differs from the `black<24` pin. A contributor fixes one line in server.py and saves. Black rewrites the whole file (81 over-length lines in that file alone), so the PR diff is mostly formatting churn and conflicts with every other open PR that touches the file.

The vscode user gets no sudo and the image has no sudo package, so nothing can be installed as root inside the running container. A developer needs `jq` (used by CI's manifest check), `openssh-client`, or a debugging tool. `apt-get install` fails with permission denied and the only option is to edit the Dockerfile and rebuild.

`pip install uv` pulls whatever uv version is newest at build time, so two contributors' containers (or a rebuild) can run different uv versions with different `uv venv` / `uv pip` behavior. A future uv release that makes replacing an existing `.venv` without `--clear` an error breaks postCreateCommand on every rebuild, with no change in this repo. Pin the version (e.g. `uv==0.9.*`) or copy it from `ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:<ver>`.

The Dockerfile rebuilds by hand what `mcr.microsoft.com/devcontainers/python:3.11` already provides: a UID-1000 `vscode` user, sudo, bash/zsh, git with openssh-client, less and curl. A uv dev container feature would cover the uv install. Maintaining a custom Dockerfile is what let the ssh-client, login-shell and sudo gaps above in. Using `"image": "mcr.microsoft.com/devcontainers/python:1-3.11-bookworm"` plus a uv feature would remove the Dockerfile and all three defects.

`ms-azuretools.vscode-docker` gets installed, but the container has no docker CLI and no mounted Docker socket (no docker-outside-of-docker feature). GitLens and Git Graph are personal-preference extensions forced on every contributor. The Docker extension activates, can't reach a daemon, and shows errors without being able to do anything. Every contributor also gets GitLens/Git Graph installed whether they want them or not, which makes container startup slower.

`build-essential` adds roughly 200+ MB (gcc, g++, make, libc dev headers), but every dependency (cryptography, bcrypt, pynacl via paramiko; uvloop and httptools via uvicorn[standard]; pydantic-core) ships manylinux wheels for CPython 3.11. Every first build and every Codespaces create downloads and unpacks a few hundred MB of compiler toolchain that nothing uses, which slows down onboarding.

`build.context` is set to the repo root even though the Dockerfile has no COPY or ADD, and the repo has no .dockerignore. With the legacy builder (or anything that sends the full context), every build ships the whole repo to the daemon, including `.venv`, `.git` and the credential-bearing `proxmox-config/config.json`. Dropping `context` (default is `.devcontainer/`) has the same result at no cost.

`"ruff.enable": true` is already the Ruff extension's default. `"remoteUser": "vscode"` repeats the Dockerfile's `USER vscode`, which Dev Containers already uses as the container user. Two settings that do nothing. They add config surface that can drift, for example if USERNAME is changed in the Dockerfile but not in devcontainer.json.

The `@AssertTrue` on `harOppgittInntekt()` never runs. Hibernate Validator only treats `get*`/`is*`/`has*` methods as bean properties, so a `har*` method is skipped by `validator.validate(bean)`. Every other `@AssertTrue` in the repo uses `isX()`. The same problem exists in `OppgittInntektForPeriode.harOppgittInntekt()`. POST /aktivitetspenger/inntektsrapportering/innsending with `{"oppgaveReferanse":"<uuid>","oppgittInntekt":{}}` passes `@Valid`. A k9 søknad with a null `arbeidstakerOgFrilansInntekt` is published and journalført, and the oppgave is marked løst with a null inntekt in `RapportertInntektDto`. The required-inntekt check never fires.

The rapportering is published to Kafka (`innsendingService.registrer`) before `markerOppgaveSomLøst`. `hentInntektsrapporteringPeriode` also never checks that the oppgave is ULØST or of type RAPPORTER_INNTEKT. A wrong oppgavetypeData throws IllegalStateException, which surfaces as a 500 instead of a 4xx. The user submits for an oppgave that is already LØST, or `markerOppgaveSomLøst` fails transiently. The inntekt is already on the mottatt topic and will be journalført, but the user gets a 500. A retry after the 10s duplicate window publishes a second rapportering and creates a duplicate journalpost/k9 søknad for the same oppgave.

`AKTIVITETSPENGER_INNTEKTRAPPORTERING` uses the placeholder brevkode `FIXME_AVP_INNTEKT_BREVKODE`. The endpoint and streams are live, and `YtelseType.enabled()` defaults to true, so nothing keeps this out of production. Once deployed, every aktivitetspenger inntektsrapportering is journalført in dokarkiv with brevkode `FIXME_AVP_INNTEKT_BREVKODE`. Downstream routing and document classification that keys on brevkode will misroute or reject these journalposts, and they are hard to fix after the fact.

The rapportering is built as an ordinary `Aktivitetspenger` søknad with `søknadsperiode` set to the inntekt period. It has no rapportering/søknadstype marker; the ungdomsytelse equivalent sets `UngSøknadstype.RAPPORTERING_SØKNAD`. It is also validated with the full `AktivitetspengerSøknadValidator`. A consumer of the k9 JSON (ung-sak reads the cleanup topic, and the JSON is journalført) sees an AKTIVITETSPENGER søknad with søknadsperiode 2025-01-01/2025-01-31 and empty forutgåendeBosteder. It cannot tell this apart from a new aktivitetspenger søknad for that month and may treat the income report as a søknad.

Two parallel topics grant `ung-brukerdialog-api` read access on their mottatt and cleanup topics: aktivitetspenger-soknad and ungdomsytelse-inntektsrapportering (the latter also grants ung-deltakelse-opplyser). The new aktivitetspenger-inntektsrapportering topics grant only ung-sak read on cleanup and no read on mottatt. If ung-brukerdialog-api consumes these topics the way it does for the søknad and ungdomsytelse rapportering flows (for example to track oppgave state), its consumer gets authorization errors on the new topics. Those events are then silently missing in that service.

`arbeidstakerOgFrilansInntekt: Int?` has no `@Min(0)`/`@PositiveOrZero` constraint, so a negative inntekt passes API validation. A request with `"arbeidstakerOgFrilansInntekt": -5000` is accepted (unless the k9 validator happens to reject it). The oppgave is marked løst with `RapportertInntektDto(..., -5000)`, which feeds a negative reported income into ung-sak's calculation.

The new aktivitetspenger controller test imports `no.nav.brukerdialog.ytelse.ungdomsytelse.utils.InntektrapporteringUtils`, so it posts a serialized `UngdomsytelseInntektsrapportering` instead of the new `AktivitetspengerInntektsrapportering` fixture. It also never checks what `markerOppgaveSomLøst` receives. If the aktivitetspenger DTO later diverges (new required field, renamed property), this test keeps passing because it serializes the ungdomsytelse class. A wrong `RapportertInntektDto` (periode or beløp) sent to ung-brukerdialog-api would also go undetected.

`PDF_PREFIX = "ung"` and the ids `1-full-inntekt-alle`/`2-arbeidstaker-og-frilansinntekt` are identical to `UngdomsytelseInntektsrapporteringPdfGeneratorTest`. The two generated cases in this test are also byte-for-byte the same input. Running the 'opprett lesbar oppsummerings-PDF' tests writes both suites to the same paths, so whichever runs last overwrites the other's PDFs. The second case adds no coverage, so a scenario such as zero or absent inntekt is never rendered.

The new producer topic `AKTIVITETSPENGER_INNTEKTSRAPPORTERING_TOPIC` was added to `Topics`/`hentTopicForYtelse` but not to `KafkaProducerService.health()`'s `partitionsFor` checks. If the topic is missing or its ACL is wrong in an environment, the producer health indicator still reports UP. The failure only appears when users submit and get `MeldingRegistreringFeiletException`.

`forsikreIkkeDuplikatInnsending` runs only after `hentInntektsrapporteringPeriode` has made a blocking HTTP call (with retries) to ung-brukerdialog-api. Every duplicate or double-clicked submission still pays a remote `hentOppgave` round-trip, plus retry/backoff on errors, before being rejected. Moving the cheap cache check (the key only needs personIdent + ytelse) before the HTTP call avoids that.

`OppgittInntekt`, `OppgittInntektForPeriode` and `UngPeriode` copy `ytelse.ungdomsytelse.api.domene.inntektsrapportering` line for line. `aktivitetspenger-rapportering-soknad.hbs` is identical to `ungdomsytelse-rapportering-soknad.hbs`, including the dead `{{ id }}` footer key, and the PdfData differs only in the ytelse class. There are two copies of the validation and k9 mapping (including the broken `har*` @AssertTrue) and two templates to keep in sync. A fix to one, such as validation, the k9 BigDecimal mapping or the template, will silently be missed in the other. Reuse the existing classes and template, or extract them to a shared package.

`inntektrapportering` and `hentInntektsrapporteringPeriode` are verbatim copies of `UngdomsytelseService.inntektrapportering`/`hentInntektsrapporteringPeriode`. Only the Innsending class differs. Fixes to oppgave validation, ordering of Kafka publish vs. markerOppgaveSomLøst, or the RapportertInntektDto mapping must be made twice. A shared helper parameterized by an Innsending factory would remove the duplication.

The bean method is named `aktivitetpengerInntektsrapporteringCleanupTopic` (missing 's'). Both consumers inject the parameter `aktivitetspengerInntektsrapporteringCleanupTopic`, so wiring depends entirely on generic-type matching rather than the bean name. If another bean with an assignable `Topic<...>` type is added, Spring can no longer fall back on the parameter name to pick a candidate. Startup then fails with NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException, and the typo makes the bean hard to find by name.

The test has leftovers from the ungdomsytelse copy. `deltakelseId` is created and passed to `preprosessertSøknadSomJson` but never used in the JSON. The controller test stubs `barnService.hentBarn()`, which the inntekt flow never calls. Readers can't tell which inputs matter, for example whether deltakelseId should appear in the payload. Leftover stubs hide which collaborators the new flow actually uses.

The "*" (keep) branch only looks up existingCred.Env under the new URL, so the UI's rename remap (`{newUrl: '*'}` with oldUrl deleted) never transfers the old URL's token, even though the comment says it handles "transferred from a renamed one". An admin has https://github.com/org/private with a token and edits it to https://github.com/org/private/dev while leaving the token field empty. The UI sends `{".../dev": "*"}`. existingCred.Env[".../dev"] doesn't exist, so newTokens is empty. The credential gets deleted and the next sync fails auth. The UI comment says an empty field leaves the credential unchanged. The fix needs an explicit old→new mapping (or index-based keys) in the API.

Update rewrites scheme-less entries in manifest.SourceURLs to https:// but leaves the keys of manifest.SourceURLCredentials as they were, so credentials sent for a scheme-less URL fail the activeURLs check and are silently thrown away. An admin adds `github.com/org/private` with token ghp_x. SourceURLs becomes ["https://github.com/org/private"] but the credential key is still "github.com/org/private". It isn't in activeURLs, so it is skipped and no credential is stored. The request still returns 200 and the private repo fails to sync with no hint why.

resolveToken compares against the hard-coded defaultCatalogURL constant instead of the configured OBOT_SERVER_DEFAULT_MCPCATALOG_PATH (h.defaultCatalogPath), so a deployment whose default catalog is a different private GitHub repo no longer gets GITHUB_AUTH_TOKEN. An operator sets OBOT_SERVER_DEFAULT_MCPCATALOG_PATH=https://github.com/acme/private-catalog plus GITHUB_AUTH_TOKEN. Before this change, sync used the token. Now resolveToken returns "", the GitHub API size check returns 404 and the clone fails auth, so the default catalog stops syncing after upgrade. Meanwhile the hard-coded obot-platform URL never needs the token for the size check (that check returns early for org obot-platform).

isGitRepoURL now classifies every gitlab.com URL as a git repo, so GitLab raw-file catalog URLs that used to be fetched over plain HTTP are now sent to parseGitURL/clone and fail. An existing source `https://gitlab.com/org/repo/-/raw/main/catalog.yaml` gets parsed as repo org/repo.git with branch `-/raw/main/catalog.yaml`. validateBranchName rejects the leading '-', so sync fails with "invalid branch name". Before this change, isGitHubURL returned false and http.Get read the YAML. API-style URLs such as /api/v4/projects/.../raw break the same way.

sizeLimitedFS shares one byte counter between the .git store (packfile, idx, index) and the uncompressed worktree checkout, so the real limit is well under the documented 100 MB and doesn't match the API pre-check that measures repo size. A repo GitHub reports as 40 MB passes checkGitHubRepoSize. But a 40 MB pack plus a 70 MB uncompressed checkout writes about 110 MB to the shared counter, so the clone aborts with "repository is too large (limit: 100 MB)" even though the repo is under the limit. Only the .git storage should count, or the limit should be documented as total disk.

Non-default GitHub sources no longer use GITHUB_AUTH_TOKEN at all. Existing deployments that relied on it for private repos or to avoid rate limits (as chart/values.yaml documents) break on upgrade, and nothing migrates them. An existing catalog source https://github.com/acme/internal-mcps worked through the server-wide PAT. After upgrade, checkGitHubRepoSize calls the API without auth, gets 404 and records a sync error. Public repos now make unauthenticated API calls (60/hr per IP, often a shared NAT IP), so syncs can fail with 403. Sync errors also skip pruning, so stale entries are left behind.

revealCatalogCredential only logs non-NotFound errors and returns "", so sync carries on without auth and SyncErrors shows a misleading auth or 404 failure. The doc comment claims these errors are "visible in the sync status", but they are not. The credential store has a brief outage or decryption error during sync. Each private source is fetched without its token and SyncErrors[url] says "authentication required" or "GitHub API returned status 404". The admin goes looking at the token or repo instead of the credential store. Returning the error and recording it in SyncErrors would show the real cause.

Update saves catalog.Spec.SourceURLs before it writes or deletes the credential, so a failed CreateCredential or DeleteCredential returns an error to the client after the URL changes have already been committed. An admin adds a private URL with a token and CreateCredential fails. The API returns 500, but the URL is already in the spec. The UI shows an error and keeps the dialog open, and retrying with Add hits "duplicate URL found". The catalog now syncs that URL without a token. Writing the credential first (or rolling back) avoids this.

List and Get now call RevealCredential for every catalog and fail the whole request on any non-NotFound error, even though they only need it for a presence marker. If the credential store is slow, down, or can't decrypt one entry, GET /api/mcp-catalogs returns 500 and the admin MCP Servers page can't load any catalog. Before this change those endpoints didn't touch credentials. Non-default catalogs can never have this credential (Update is default-only) but are still looked up on every List.

When no branch is given, parseGitURL defaults to refs/heads/main instead of the remote HEAD. Now that self-hosted and GitLab repos are supported, repos whose default branch is master or something else fail to clone. https://git.example.com/org/catalog.git has default branch `master`. The clone asks for refs/heads/main and fails with "reference not found". Leaving ReferenceName empty when no branch is given (with SingleBranch) would follow the remote HEAD.

isGitRepoURL accepts `https://host/repo.git`, but parseGitURL requires at least two path segments, so root-level self-hosted repos are routed to the git path and then always rejected. https://git.example.com/catalog.git (common with cgit/gitweb/Gitea-style hosting) gets "invalid git URL format, expected <host>/org/repo" even though the URL ends in .git as the docs require. Before this change it would at least have been tried as a raw file.

Sync calls revealCatalogCredential inside the per-URL loop, and each call reveals the same single credential that holds every token. A catalog with N source URLs does N identical credential-store reveals (each a decrypt and round trip) every hourly sync and every forced refresh. Revealing once before the loop and indexing Env[sourceURL] does the same job.

checkGitHubRepoSize calls resolveToken again on a token that readGitCatalog has already resolved. The fallback can never fire, because the only matching URL (obot-platform/mcp-catalog) returns early on the org check, and the doc comment ("Falls back to the GITHUB_AUTH_TOKEN env var if no per-URL token is provided") is wrong. The token logic is spread across two places and the comment misleads readers about when the env token is used. Use the passed-in token directly and fix the comment.

readGitCatalog parses the URL itself, calls parseGitURL (which parses it again), then rebuilds repoPath by trimming the https://host/ prefix and .git suffix off cloneURL. Also, readGitCatalog's doc comment ended up on parseGitURL (line 212). The string round-trip is fragile and duplicates parseGitURL's work. parseGitURL could return host and repoPath directly. The misplaced comment leaves parseGitURL's doc starting with "readGitCatalog clones…" and readGitCatalog with no doc.

The new credential-merge logic in Update (keep/clear/new/rename/normalization) and resolveToken have no tests. The rename-drops-token and scheme-less-key bugs above would each be caught by a simple table test of the merge. Without tests, later changes to this sentinel-based protocol can silently delete stored tokens.

parseGitHubUrl matches `tree/<branch>` but throws the branch away, so resolveIdentifier always installs from the repository's default branch. `spm install https://github.com/org/repo/tree/develop/path/to/skill` calls fetchDefaultBranch and resolves `ref: 'main'`, so it fetches main's skillset.yml (wrong content) or 404s if the path only exists on develop. The new test 'parses GitHub URL with non-main branch' asserts this lossy result. SkillIdentifier needs an optional `ref`, and resolveIdentifier should use it and skip the GitHub API call when it is present.

Path containment is broken in two ways: `resolved.startsWith(baseDir)` has no trailing-separator check, and `tmpDir` is built from the untrusted manifest `skillset.name` without validation. A manifest with `name: ../../../Users/<author>/.claude` makes tmpDir resolve outside the system temp dir, and safePath only checks against that already-escaped base, so files get written there. Separately, with `name: fsd`, an `agents` entry like `../../../fsd-x/evil` resolves to `/tmp/spm/fsd-x/evil`, which still passes `startsWith('/tmp/spm/fsd')`. Validate name against something like /^[\w.-]+$/ and compare with `baseDir + sep` (or use path.relative).

Every entry is downloaded with `location.ref`, the default branch of the skillset's own repo, including cross-repo `@owner/repo/path` skills that live in other repositories. Skillset repo `org/skillbox` uses `main` and a skill source is `@other/lib/skills/x` whose default branch is `master`. The fetch goes to raw.githubusercontent.com/other/lib/main/... and returns 404, so the whole install fails. FileEntry carries no per-repo ref, so cross-repo skills can't work unless both repos share a branch name.

The regex assumes a single-segment branch and captures everything after it, including a trailing slash, query string or fragment, into the path. `.../tree/feature/new-skill/claude/fsd` gets branch=`feature` and path=`new-skill/claude/fsd`, giving a 404. `.../tree/main/claude/fsd/` (copied from the browser) gives path `claude/fsd/` and then `claude/fsd//skillset.yml`. `...?tab=readme` puts the query into the path. `www.github.com` URLs and repo-root URLs (`/tree/main` with no path) are rejected.

Downloads go to a predictable, shared `os.tmpdir()/spm/<name>` directory. Nothing clears it first, and mkdir/writeFile follow symlinks. On a multi-user host, another user can pre-create `/tmp/spm/fsd` as a symlink to the victim's directory, and the recursive mkdir plus writeFile then write through it. Even single-user, files left over from an earlier version of the skillset stay next to the new ones, and two concurrent installs of the same skillset overwrite each other. Use mkdtemp (or write into the project's provider dir) and clean up.

The traversal guard runs only in the bare-path branch, so `./` sources, `@` sources, `files[]`, `setup`, and agents/hooks/rules entries can still contain `..`. The substring test also rejects legitimate names like `foo..bar`. `source: './../../other'` or `files: ['../../../x']` pass unchecked. Because the WHATWG URL parser normalizes `..` in the raw.githubusercontent URL, they fetch arbitrary paths, and they reach the local write path that safePath guards imperfectly. Meanwhile a skill dir named `v1..2` is wrongly rejected. Validating each final entry path once, per segment (`seg === '..'`), in resolveSkillset is the general fix.

The old 'Invalid skill source' error is gone. Any string that isn't `./` or `@` is now treated as a repo-root path, including empty strings and URLs. `source: ''` gives basePath '' and entry path `/SKILL.md`. The raw URL gets a `//`, and safePath resolves `/SKILL.md` as absolute and throws a misleading 'Path traversal detected'. `source: 'https://example.com/x'` turns into the path `https:/example.com/x` and 404s instead of reporting a clear validation error. Typos like `.claude/skill` (meant `./`) silently resolve to the wrong place.

validateSkillset checks only the four top-level string fields. Now that install consumes `skills[].source`, `skills[].files`, `setup`, and agents/hooks, a malformed manifest crashes with an opaque TypeError. A manifest with `skills: { git: { source: './git' } }` (no `files`) prints `✖ Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'forEach')`. With `source: 123` it prints `source.startsWith is not a function`. With `agents: 'a.md'` (a string, not a list) it prints `files.forEach is not a function`. None of these points the user at the bad manifest field.

The output layout uses only `entry.path` and ignores owner/repository, and all writes run concurrently, so two entries that map to the same path race silently. Skill `@a/lib/skills/x` and skill `@b/lib/skills/x` both produce `skills/x/SKILL.md`, and the same happens if a file is listed twice. The two concurrent `writeFile` calls to one path leave whichever finishes last, and the success line still reports both as downloaded.

The install action is now async, but the program still calls `program.parse()` rather than `await program.parseAsync()`, which Commander requires for async action handlers. The returned promise is not awaited by Commander. Today it only works because the action's try/catch swallows everything. Any rejection that escapes it, or any future post-parse code such as hooks or exit handling, runs before install finishes, and unhandled rejections bypass the formatted error output.

downloadFromGitHub re-implements the raw.githubusercontent.com URL construction already in fetchSkillset (fetch-skillset.ts:26), and neither encodes path segments. Two copies of the URL and error logic will drift; fetchSkillset could just call downloadFromGitHub. A file named `notes#1.md` or `a?b.md` has its path cut off as a fragment or query, and names with `%` or spaces fetch the wrong resource. Map each segment through encodeURIComponent.

The downloader tests stub `fetch` with `vi.stubGlobal` but tear down with `vi.restoreAllMocks()`, which does not restore stubbed globals. The `mkdtempSync` temp dirs are never removed. After each test (and after the file, if isolation is ever turned off), the global `fetch` stays mocked, so later tests that expect real or differently stubbed fetch behavior see the stale mock. Use `vi.unstubAllGlobals()` (or `unstubGlobals: true` in config). The same pattern is in download-from-url.test.ts and download-file.test.ts, which also leave temp dirs behind in the OS temp directory.

`__VERSION__` is defined only in vite.config.ts. vitest.config.ts takes precedence for tests and lacks the define, and the CLI version test was loosened to accept any semver. Any unit test that imports src/bin/spm.ts (directly or transitively) fails with `ReferenceError: __VERSION__ is not defined`. The integration test now passes even if the build embeds the wrong version (for example a stale dist or a broken define), because it no longer compares against package.json's version.

The committed `.spmrc.yml` looks like the artifact `readConfig()` writes into the git root when the integration test runs `spm install`; it is not a real config for this CLI tool's repo. The integration test runs the built CLI from the repo, so readConfig auto-creates `.spmrc.yml` at the git root, and that file was committed. With it committed, the test no longer exercises the create-config path, and every developer's clone carries a config that detectProviders would regenerate differently based on local folders.

downloadEntries wraps every entry in a GitHubSource, sends it through the generic downloadFile dispatcher, then spreads the result (carrying an unused `source`) and overwrites `path`. safePath also calls `normalize` before `resolve`, which already normalizes. Every entry is always GitHub, so `downloadFromGitHub({...})` returning `{ type, path, content }` does the same job with fewer layers. The URL and local downloaders (and their exports) have no producer anywhere, so they are dead code for now that still has to be maintained and tested.

The hand-written Deployment omits `envFrom: secretRef: ms-secret-vault`, which the shared chart template always injected, so the agent no longer gets any Vault-sourced secrets. backend/ai-secure-agent-config.yaml sets mysql user `root` with no password, and the other services' configs note that credentials come from ms-secret-vault. With this manifest the pod starts without the DB password, LLM/API keys, or other Vault secrets, so MySQL/Redis/LLM calls fail on auth or the app crashes at startup.

agent-app uses `targetRevision: AI-20-AISecureAgent-Feature-collection` while every other Application tracks HEAD, so production deploys of the agent follow a feature branch. Once this merges to main, edits to agent/ on main (tag bumps, env fixes) never deploy. When the feature branch is deleted after merge, agent-app goes to ComparisonError/Unknown and stops reconciling. The ConfigMap it mounts is still served from HEAD by backend-app, so config and Deployment come from different revisions.

agent-app renders the same Deployment `ai-secure-agent-ms` and Service `ai-secure-agent-ms-svc` that the helm-app ApplicationSet still generates from `revision: HEAD` until this lands on main, and both have automated selfHeal. If app-of-apps.yaml is applied from this branch (which the feature-branch targetRevision implies), helm-app (main) and agent-app (feature branch) keep overwriting each other's pod template: endless rollouts plus a SharedResourceWarning. After merge, the ApplicationSet deletes the generated `ai-secure-agent-ms` Application. Its default resources finalizer cascade-deletes the same-named Deployment/Service, which races with agent-app and causes an outage until the next re-sync.

MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI targets `mlflow-tracking-svc.mlflow.svc.cluster.local:5000`, but the only MLflow Service in the repo is `mlflow` in namespace mlflow on port 80 (targetPort 5000). With ENABLE_MLFLOW_TRACING=true, every trace export does a DNS lookup for mlflow-tracking-svc, gets NXDOMAIN, and fails. Traces are lost, and depending on the client the app either logs errors and adds latency per request or fails at startup. The value should be http://mlflow.mlflow.svc.cluster.local (port 80).

The agent repo's CI bumps image.tag in helm_backend/ai-secure-agent-ms/values.yaml (see cffc861), but this change deletes that file and hardcodes the tag in a raw manifest the CI does not touch. On the next agent build, the CI either fails, or recreates helm_backend/ai-secure-agent-ms/values.yaml holding only image.tag. The ApplicationSet then regenerates an `ai-secure-agent-ms` app from chart defaults (user-ms configmap and probe path, linkerd enabled, grpc port) that collides with agent-app. Either way the image at line 20 never updates.

The old liveness and readiness probes on `/ai-secure-agent-ms/v1/ping` were not carried over to the new Deployment. The Service sends traffic to the pod as soon as the container starts, before config/Kafka/MySQL init finishes, so early requests fail. A hung or deadlocked process is never restarted, and rolling updates mark a broken new pod Available right away and kill the old healthy one.

The previous resource settings (requests 100m/256Mi, limits 200m/345Mi, tuned in de07dae alongside MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2) are gone, so the pod runs BestEffort and unbounded. On the small k3s node the agent becomes the first pod evicted under memory pressure. A memory leak or large LLM payload can grow without limit and OOM neighbors or the node instead of just restarting this container. The scheduler also ignores its real footprint.

The chart mounted a hostPath /tmp/logs/ai-secure-agent-ms at /app/logs, with a fix-perm initContainer that chmods it; the new manifest has neither. If the app writes to /app/logs, as the shared convention expects, logs now land on the ephemeral container filesystem and are lost on every restart, or writes fail when the directory is missing or not writable for a non-root user. Anything reading /tmp/logs/* on the host loses this service's logs.

Instead of keeping the service on the shared charts/ templates (and making grpc/log pieces optional there), the diff copies the Deployment/Service by hand into a separate Application, re-implementing what charts/templates/deployment.yaml and service.yaml already provide. The fork already silently dropped secrets, probes, resources, the log volume and anti-affinity, which is the drift the shared chart exists to prevent. Each future chart fix (e.g. probe defaults) now has to be repeated by hand here. Adding `if` guards for grpcPort and applogs in the chart, and overriding targetRevision on the existing helm app for preview, would meet the same goal without the fork.

The Service and container no longer expose the `grpc` port 5001 that the chart previously published for ai-secure-agent-ms-svc. Any client calling ai-secure-agent-ms-svc:5001 (the convention every other backend uses) now gets connection refused. No in-repo caller was found, so this only matters if another repo or service dials the gRPC port.

The previous values explicitly set `linkerd.io/inject: disabled` (added in de07dae); the new pod template has no annotation, so whether the pod is meshed now depends on the namespace. The default namespace has no annotation today, so nothing changes yet. If someone enables namespace-level injection (the usual linkerd setup), this pod silently gets a proxy sidecar, bringing back whatever issue the explicit opt-out was added to avoid.

The diff turns app-of-apps.yaml from a file ending in a newline into one without (agent/ai-secure-agent.yaml also lacks one). Appending the next Application with `cat >>`/`echo >>`, a common habit for this multi-doc file, produces `- CreateNamespace=true---`. That is valid YAML but a different string, so the separator is lost and the next Application merges into or breaks this document.

Cluster mode picks a URL from status.endpoints, but the operator always writes in-cluster service DNS there (http://{name}-keycloak.{ns}.svc.cluster.local:8080, keycloak_reconciler.py:464-467). A workstation outside the cluster cannot resolve that host. Running the headline docs example (`--keycloak my-keycloak --namespace keycloak-system --realm my-realm` with no --server-url) from a laptop: the token POST to http://my-keycloak-keycloak.keycloak-system.svc.cluster.local:8080 fails with a DNS 'no such host' error. The comment's 'admin > public > internal because we run outside the cluster' reasoning does not hold, since all three are cluster-internal URLs. Cluster mode only works with --server-url or from inside the cluster.

The double-base64 heuristic decodes any secret value whose length is a multiple of 4 and that uses only base64 characters. That corrupts real credentials, including about 14% of operator-generated passwords. The operator makes 16-char passwords from letters, digits and !@#$%^&* (utils/kubernetes.py:1428-1429). When none of the special characters appear ((62/70)^16 ≈ 14%), isBase64 returns true and DecodeString succeeds, so the tool sends 12 garbage bytes as the password and gets 401. Usernames like 'user', 'root' or 'test' in an existingSecret are corrupted the same way. The operator decodes secret data exactly once (keycloak_reconciler.py:1315-1320), so the toolkit must not decode again.

Keycloak's PartialImportResults JSON has no `errors` field (it has added/skipped/overwritten/results/errorMessage), and result actions are only ADDED/SKIPPED/OVERWRITTEN. Errors is therefore always 0 and the 'hard fail on errors > 0' path can never fire. Any batch Keycloak accepts is treated as clean. The ERROR/FAILED action filter and the `batchResult.Errors > 0` branch (line 90) are dead code. Real failures arrive only as non-200 statuses with errorMessage. The design in ADR-093 and the docs ('Any batch response with errors > 0 causes an immediate hard failure') describes behaviour that does not exist.

The response struct never parses `overwritten`, and ImportResult and the summary have no Overwritten count. In --mode overwrite, every replaced user disappears from the totals. Re-running with --mode overwrite against a realm where all 5,000 users exist prints 'Added: 0, Skipped: 0, Errors: 0' for 5,000 total users. That looks like nothing happened, when every user was actually overwritten.

When importBatch, a token refresh or authentication fails, the function returns a nil result, which throws away the Added/Skipped totals from batches that already finished. The caller's 'print partial result so user can see progress' code then prints nothing. Batch 7 of 10 returns HTTP 500. The user gets 'batch 7/10 failed: ...' and no summary, even though batches 1-6 committed 3,000 users. Because the errors>0 path never fires, this nil-result path is the only failure path in practice, so the partial-progress handling in import_users.go:161-163 never runs.

Every HTTP call uses http.DefaultClient (no timeout) with a context.Background() context that has no deadline and no signal handling (import_users.go:88), so a stalled server or load balancer hangs the import forever. An ingress that accepts the connection but never responds to a 500-user partialImport POST, or a half-open TCP connection, blocks the process with no timeout. Nothing reports which batch was in flight.

The admin password is only accepted as a --password command-line flag, so it shows up in `ps`/`/proc/<pid>/cmdline` and in shell history. No environment variable or stdin option exists. In the documented CI example `--password "$KEYCLOAK_ADMIN_PASSWORD"`, the shell expands the value into argv, so any other user or process on the host can read the master-realm admin password from the process table while the import runs.

The fallback URL is built from `spec.hostname` and `spec.tls.enabled`, but the Keycloak CRD has no spec.hostname. The externally reachable host is spec.ingress.host (with ingress.tlsEnabled), and spec.tls.enabled is pod-level TLS, not ingress TLS. KeycloakSpec.Hostname is always empty, so this branch is dead and the 'spec.hostname is not set' error points users at a field that does not exist. The ingress host, which is what an off-cluster tool needs, is never consulted.

The 409 error message always says '(mode=FAIL)', but Keycloak also returns 409 in SKIP/OVERWRITE mode, for example when an imported user's email clashes with an existing user that has a different username (ModelDuplicateException). A user runs with the default --mode skip and gets 'HTTP 409 Conflict (mode=FAIL)'. They conclude the mode flag was ignored, when the real cause is a duplicate email.

Readiness is a strict `phase == "Ready"` check, which rejects Degraded (and transient Reconciling) instances where Keycloak is still serving. The operator itself treats Degraded as operational (drift_detection_service.py:320). A Keycloak instance in Degraded because an unrelated realm failed to reconcile blocks the import with 'is not Ready', even though the admin API works. This is also true when --server-url is supplied explicitly.

The docs and ADR-093 say Partial Import is non-atomic per batch. In fact Keycloak's PartialImportManager marks the transaction rollback-only on any error, so each request is all-or-nothing. Operators size --batch-size and plan recovery based on wrong semantics. They expect a failed batch to have partly committed, when actually the whole batch rolled back, and the ADR's rejected-alternative rationale rests on this claim.

Only `chunk` and the loader are tested. importBatch, authenticate, resolveURL, decodeSecretKey/isBase64 and the token-refresh logic have no tests, though httptest makes them cheap to cover. A single httptest case with a real Keycloak PartialImportResults body would have caught the missing `errors`/`overwritten` fields. A table test of decodeSecretKey with an alphanumeric 16-char password would have caught the base64 corruption.

The library package writes progress and dry-run output straight to stdout with fmt.Printf, while the command writes through cmd.Printf, which cobra sends to stderr by default. The output is split across two streams and can't be redirected or captured in tests. `keycloak-migrate import-users ... --dry-run > plan.txt` puts the dry-run plan in the file while 'Loading...' and the summary go to the terminal. Tests cannot capture importer output via cmd.SetOut.

currentKubeNamespace builds its own kubeconfig loader that duplicates the one in ResolveFromCluster. Its `ns == ""` → "default" fallback is also redundant, because clientcmd's Namespace() already returns "default". Kubeconfig is loaded and parsed twice per run, and the two loaders can drift (for example if one later honours --context/--kubeconfig flags and the other doesn't). Simpler form: have ResolveFromCluster accept an empty namespace and resolve it from the same ClientConfig.

users.json is parsed twice: once into json.RawMessage just to check the first byte is '[', then again into []map[string]any. Unmarshalling into the slice already rejects objects and scalars with a type error. For a 50k-user export with credential hashes (tens to hundreds of MB), the extra scan and copy doubles parse time and peak memory for no added validation. Simpler form: a single json.Unmarshal into []map[string]any, wrapping the UnmarshalTypeError with the 'must contain a JSON array' message.
